newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Krupp sees better oper profit in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Krupp sees better oper profit in 1997.

text.p: German engineering group Krupp, in the throes of merging its steel operations with rival Thyssen AG, said on Wednesday it expected to post a better operating profit and pay a dividend again in 1997.

Discussions with Thyssen were proceeding constructively, and the merged steel venture should show an operating profit this year, Gerhard Cromme, chairman of Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, told the company's annual news conference.
Krupp's 1997 result would again ensure a dividend after a difficult 1996 when profit dropped by nearly half due to soft steel prices and weak domestic demand, Cromme said.
In April Krupp reported revenue from ordinary activities in 1996 of 336 million marks ($197 million), down from 644 million marks the year before.
Net profit tumbled to 208 million marks from 505 million marks. It paid an unchanged dividend of five marks. Steel was the only one of its divisions in the red.
Chief finance officer Gerhard Jooss said domestic business showed a loss of over 200 million marks last year, and that all profit came from operations outside Germany.
Krupp, which first launched a takeover bid for Thyssen before settling on the limited merger, also expected business volume to expand this year, Cromme said.

"Krupp is confident it can make use of the improved economic situation and continued good export demand to broaden its business volume," Cromme said. But steel prices must continue recovering from their plunge last year.

Plans were to make the merger retroactive to April 1, 1997, and Krupp might have to pay Thyssen an unspecified sum to balance the shares at the agreed 60-40, with Krupp holding the smaller share, Cromme said.
"The future, joint, capable enterprise (Thyssen Krupp Stahl) will have the necessary size to reach internationally competitive costs and adequate market share," he said.

The new steel company would finance its restructuring from synergies, but the structural costs could not yet be specified, he said. One condition for the merger was that Thyssen should not be worse off than it would have been on its own. Krupp had agreed to provide the up-front financing for the merger, Cromme said.
The agreement must be completed by the end of September.
Krupp's orders and sales showed an uptrend in the first three months of the year, with orders rising 5.6 percent from the year earlier level to 6.5 billion marks.
Cromme said Krupp was actively preparing for the introduction of the single European currency, scheduled for January 1999.
Monetary union would help to cut costs for procurement, hedging and currency transactions, make planning more secure and give it access to a deeper capital market, he said.

Foreign business accounted for 60 percent of Krupp's business, and would continue to increase, Cromme said. Markets for Krupp's high-tech industrial products were not growing in Germany, but were elsewhere, particularly in Asia.
Krupp had to expand operations in those markets or be left behind, Cromme said.
